feed.title: package-trends releases
feed.subtitle: npm download trends as a sparkline, a calendar heatmap, a line of text, or a KPI block. Compare packages, repair npm's missing days. Zero dependencies, works without a proxy.

entry.title: package-trends 0.2.0
entry.content:
Minor Changes

  • A calendar heatmap: one square per day, one column per week, from a new /heatmap entry. <PackageHeatmap> in React, heatmapSvg() for a string, and heatmapGeometry() for the squares as data — all three drawing from one computation, so a server render and the client agree square for square.

    It shows the two things a sparkline averages away: where in the year a quiet stretch fell, and the weekday rhythm. Across react's last year Wednesday averages 20.6M against Saturday's 11.3M.

    The ramp is opacity over currentColor, so lightness alone carries the value: it inherits the surrounding text colour, inverts on a dark ground with no second palette, and survives monochrome. emptyColor gives the quietest level a colour of its own for GitHub's two-tone look. scale defaults to "linear" spanning zero, because "quantile" fills the ramp evenly and so draws a year that doubled and a year that never moved identically. Days npm reported nothing for are hatched rather than shaded, since a solid square would state a number nobody measured.

Patch Changes

  • computeTrend, compare and analyse all answered nonsense for a range with no points. The first two threw a raw TypeError, and a throw inside a React render takes the whole tree with it — on a server that is the page, not the chart. analyse was quieter and worse: NaN for mean and median, and undefined for peak and trough behind a type promising a DownloadPoint.

    All three now throw PackageTrendsError with the package named, and the hooks route a failed derivation into the error state they already had, so renderError handles it like any other failure. Renderers are unchanged: sparkline and heatmapGeometry can honestly draw nothing, and <PackageHeatmap> now shows its fallback rather than a zero-sized <svg>.

    svgProps is typed to accept the data-* attributes its own documentation promised; the type had been rejecting them.

entry.title: package-trends 0.1.0
entry.content:
Minor Changes

  • Column charts, a fixed domain so two charts can be compared, point marks, settable up/down colours, and analyse() for writing about a series programmatically.

    Adds a styles object for weight, display and spacing; numberFormat and percentFormat taking Intl.NumberFormat options; interactive for pointer and keyboard inspection; aggregate: "month"; between() for an explicit date range; a band chart of each period's low, mean and high; CSS lengths for width and height so a chart can scale with its text; curve for smooth, stepped or straight lines; strokeDasharray, pathProps and fillPattern for patterned charts; and svgProps for anything else the <svg> should carry.

    Also repairs the zeros npm reports for days it has no data for. Taken literally they understate the mean by a quarter and invert the weekday profile; they are now interpolated, and listed in gapDays.

  • Compare several packages at once, from a new /compare entry: <PackageComparison> as an overlaid chart or a row each, compare() and indexSeries() in the core, and fetchMany so a page asks for each distinct name only once.

    scale="indexed" restates each series against its own start, which is the only honest way to put packages of very different sizes on one chart.

  • First release. npm download trends as a sparkline, a line of text or a KPI block, with a framework-agnostic core and a React entry. Pass data from a server-side fetchDownloads to render without a request per visitor.
